input_oneliner: 45M found down at home ~12h, admitted for alcohol withdrawal, Cr 3.4 on admission labs, urine dark brown

reference_targets_freetext.item: Compartment exam: palpate limb and gluteal compartments for tense, tender swelling; pain with passive stretch; distal pulses and sensation
reference_targets_freetext.rationale: Compartment syndrome after prolonged immobility drives muscle injury and needs surgical evaluation

reference_targets_freetext.item: Inspect pressure points (sacrum, hips, heels, shoulders) for skin breakdown
reference_targets_freetext.rationale: Pressure necrosis marks the down-time and adds a source of muscle and skin injury

reference_targets_freetext.item: Orthostatic vital signs (supine to standing at 1 and 3 min)
reference_targets_freetext.rationale: Prolonged down time and alcohol withdrawal produce hypovolemia; postural pulse increment is the most specific bedside sign and sets fluid targets (McGee 1999)
Completes the volume assessment; skin turgor omitted as it performs poorly in adults

reference_targets_freetext.item: Ask: exact down time, seizure at onset, substances or medications taken, and muscle pain or weakness
reference_targets_freetext.rationale: Duration of immobility and seizure activity predict the magnitude of muscle injury
Retention is a cheap reversible contributor to oliguric AKI in an encephalopathic patient

reference_targets_freetext.item: Medication review (MAR): NSAIDs, statins, contrast, new antibiotics
reference_targets_freetext.rationale: Drug exposures raise ATN or interstitial nephritis

reference_targets_freetext.item: Ask about urine volume since admission
reference_targets_freetext.rationale: Oliguria grades severity and tracks response to fluids

off_bedside_acceptable: Urinalysis with microscopy and urine myoglobin
Basic metabolic panel, potassium, phosphate, calcium
Surgical consult if compartment syndrome suspected
should_not_recommend: Deferring the compartment exam until CK results

perturbation_pair.changed_feature: found down ~12 h -> 7 days of high-dose NSAID, no fall
perturbation_pair.input_oneliner: 45M, no fall, taking ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for a week for back pain, admitted for alcohol withdrawal, Cr 3.4 on admission labs, urine dark brown
perturbation_pair.expected_change: NSAID nephropathy/AIN/ATN rise: rash, fever timing, and arthralgia questions become must-have, orthostatic vital signs stay must-have, and the medication review (MAR) rises to must-have; compartment exam, pressure-point inspection, and the down-time question drop. Dark urine is retained deliberately as a red herring (concentrated or bilirubin-tinged urine versus myoglobinuria), so the urine-volume question should persist.
